newsitem.title: USA: Miami's Nicaraguan community fears deportation wave.
newsitem.headline: Miami's Nicaraguan community fears deportation wave.

text.p: Thousands of Nicaraguans who fled war and political turmoil in their country in the 1980s are threatened with imminent deportation from the United States under new immigration laws.

Community leaders say Nicaraguans who have called Miami home for years are now living in fear of raids or deportation letters from the Immigration and Naturalisation Service as April 1 nears, when a law which tightens the process of appeals against deportation comes into affect.
Among them are ex-guerrillas of the contra army created by the United States to fight a proxy war against the leftist Sandinista government which ruled Nicaragua from 1979 to 1990.
"They used us to fight their war and now they are throwing us on the garbage," Nestor Nunez of the Resistencia Nicaraguense told Reuters.

Like the Cubans before them, Nicaraguan exiles and refugees flocked to Miami in the 1980s to escape political convulsions and repression, settling in areas like Sweetwater and east Little Havana. Many have prospered in business.

Many but not all were given citizenship. Because of the implications for Washington's Central America policy, they were denied refugee status and lived in legal limbo, allowed to work and pay taxes but denied permanent residence.

The U.S. government now says they must return as Nicaragua has become a democracy. At least 45,000 people in the Miami area are threatened, according to the Fraternidad Nicaraguense, a coalition of community groups.
Some have lived here for many years, own homes and have children born and in school here, Fraternidad director Nora Britton-Sandigo said.
"It is catastrophic for our community," she said.
Although the INS says there will be no mass deportations, Nicaraguans are moving from house to house and hiding with friends or relatives, she said.
Having built lives here, they do not want to return to a homeland which is still in a state of political instability and where shortages in jobs and housing are acute, she said.

Several hundred people have been deported in the past two years and many more and are now receiving letters. A few weeks ago a mother of three young children who was married to a Cuban-born U.S. citizen was put on a plane for Managua.

The feeling of betrayal and abandonment is heightened because of the United States' deep involvement in Nicaragua in 1980s, when Ronald Reagan's government declared Central America a front-line against communism.

"The contra war was funded and masterminded by the United States for U.S. national security interests and so it didn't have to send its own troops down there," said businessman Jose Lagos. "Now the widows and children are told 'go home'."
Nunez, a contra intelligence officer on the Honduran border in 1981-82, said many ex-guerrillas now living in Miami worried they would be affected.
"They feel very down, angry. Some of these people are amputees and war wounded," he said.
Max Castro, a University of Miami political analyst, said the Nicaraguans were the fall guys of a confused U.S. policy.

During the war years, some administration officials wanted Nicaraguans to stay in their country in the hope they would join or support the contras. It was embarassing to admit people to the United States as refugees from a war which Washington was funding yet it could not deny them asylum from Sandinsta rule.
"The situation now is the last vestige of that contradiction," Castro said.

Their plight was coming to a head at time of rising anti-immigrant sentiment in the United States, he said. A series of new laws has come into force and a beefing up of the INS meant cases were being dealth with faster," he said.
"They've come to the end of the line. It's going to be very difficult to find an overall solution to this problem."
Letters to President Bill Clinton have been to no avail.
